stemMd: In the final paragraph the author offers an alternative to the usual reading of the clauses that subordinate the statute to ancient custom. On that alternative reading, the clauses indicate that the drafters:
instructionsMd: Answer on the basis of the passage only.

options.label: A
options.textMd: doubted that their written text would operate as they intended.

options.label: B
options.textMd: meant to preserve the authority of the elders indefinitely.

options.label: C
options.textMd: expected trained jurists to take over the drafting of statutes.

options.label: D
options.textMd: had already stopped applying customary law by the twelfth century.

explanationMd:
The paragraph sets up a contrast and then asks you to carry it: the clauses are "usually read as evidence of continuity", but "may equally be read as evidence of **anxiety**". The question asks what that second reading amounts to.

The author spells it out in the next clause: "a drafter who feels the need to subordinate his text to something older is a drafter who suspects the text will not behave as he intends." Strip the rhetoric and that is precisely option A — the clause is a symptom of the drafter’s own doubt about his text.

**How to check.** Test your answer against the signal word. "Anxiety" must be anxiety *about something*, and the only candidate in the sentence is the text’s future behaviour. Then check that your answer is the *alternative* reading and not the usual one: "continuity" would be an answer about preserving the old order, which is what the author is arguing against here, so any option pointing that way is the reading being displaced rather than the one being proposed.

distractorRationale.b: This is the "continuity" reading the author explicitly sets aside, dressed in the passage’s own vocabulary about elders. The question asks for the alternative reading that the author puts in its place, so this option answers the opposite of what was asked.
distractorRationale.d: This contradicts the passage. The clauses exist precisely because customary law was still being applied — they direct that it govern where the statute is silent — and the passage places the disappearance of the clauses within two generations of the first written statute books, not before those books were written.
distractorRationale.c: The passage does say jurists came to interpret the surviving clauses and to hold new authority, but it says only that the drafters "seem to have half-understood" this, and it never mentions jurists taking over drafting. The option turns a half-understanding of what happened into a prediction about who would draft.

accessibilityText: A question about the accompanying history passage, asking what the final paragraph’s alternative reading of the ancient-custom clauses says about the people who drafted the statutes.

provenance.notes: Original item written against an original passage.

review.author: bocconi-law-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The alternative reading treats the clauses as evidence of anxiety: the drafter suspects the text will not behave as he intends, which is (a). (b) restates something closer to the usual continuity reading and adds 'indefinitely', which the passage does not support. (c) is not attributed to the drafters. (d) contradicts the clauses' instruction to follow custom.
